title: Trait filter review: 40 v1 traits -> 18 v2 traits

model_annotations.files_note: The review used the 36 per-model annotation files, merged into one local combined_ap.json. The local per-model files are byte-identical (sha256) to those at this commit. The combined_ap.json at this commit is NOT the file used (it was removed in the next commit); later commits add further models that are not part of this review.

human_study.commit_title: Add further AI annotators to human annotations dataset
human_study.description: 101 LMArena (2024) comparisons of the Feedback Forensics paper's human study (Appendix G.2), 10 traits, 2 human annotators

data.earlier_round: A first pass used data/v2 (27 models, Gemini-2.5-Flash, single vote); its results were replaced by this v3 analysis and are not in this file.

criteria: rarely relevant on the dataset (mostly insignificant strength values)
feels odd relative to the other traits

definitions.relevance_share: share of comparisons where the annotator picked one response in both response orders
definitions.both_rate: share of comparisons where the annotator said both responses show the trait equally
definitions.order_disagreement_rate: share of all comparisons where the two response orders gave different votes (no vote kept)
definitions.order_dependent_share: order disagreements / (order disagreements + relevant comparisons); flag order_dependent at >= 0.6
definitions.strength: per model vs the reference: (n target model picked - n reference picked) / n comparisons, i.e. relevance x Cohen's kappa with chance agreement 0.5
definitions.significant: one-tailed binomial test of agreement vs disagreement as in the app, p < 0.05 / 1440 (Bonferroni over traits x models); flag rarely_relevant at <= 5 of 36 models
definitions.closest_traits: 4 traits with highest absolute vote correlation (votes coded +1 / 0 / -1 over all comparisons)
definitions.same_pick_when_both_relevant: share of comparisons where both are relevant and pick the same response
definitions.model_profile_correlation: Pearson correlation of the per-model strengths of two traits
definitions.kappa_combined: Cohen's kappa over three labels (response A, response B, not relevant): mixes relevance and pick; flag low_human_agreement below 0.2
definitions.kappa_relevance: Cohen's kappa on relevant vs not relevant only
definitions.flags: rarely_relevant, order_dependent and low_human_agreement are computed; duplicate_group and odd_one_out are judgements

duplicate_groups.name: Length
duplicate_groups.note: Exact opposites: when both are relevant they pick opposite responses in 100% of cases, and the model profiles correlate at −0.99. One of them carries all the information. Which one is close to a coin flip.

duplicate_groups.name: Formatting
duplicate_groups.note: Bold/italics picks the same response as structured formatting in 95% of shared cases (profile correlation 0.93). Numbered list is a narrower sub-case: 70% of its relevant cases are also structured-formatting cases, with the same pick in 87%.
kept: uses more bold and italics text

duplicate_groups.name: Engagement
duplicate_groups.note: 94% of follow-up-question cases are also “actively engages” cases, with the same pick in 98%. The reverse is only 53%: “actively engages” also fires on friendliness and direct address.
kept: more actively engages with the user

duplicate_groups.name: Warmth
duplicate_groups.note: 87% of polite cases and 88% of empathetic cases are also friendlier-tone cases, with the same pick in 93% and 96%.
deleted: is more empathetic to the user

duplicate_groups.name: Positive affect
duplicate_groups.note: Enthusiastic and “expresses more emotion” pick the same response in 96% of shared cases (profile correlation 0.93), with similar relevance. Optimistic is covered by either of them in 77% of its cases.

duplicate_groups.name: Agreement with the user
duplicate_groups.note: All three pick the same response in 98–100% of shared cases. None is relevant in more than 2.5% of comparisons and none is significant for more than one model.
deleted: agrees with user even if factually incorrect

duplicate_groups.name: Refusal
duplicate_groups.note: Same response picked in 100% of shared cases. Both are rare on this prompt set: 1.3% and 2.4% of comparisons.

duplicate_groups.name: Unsafe language
duplicate_groups.note: Each is relevant in at most 6 of 15,644 comparisons, so the choice between them does not matter on this data.

traits.name: uses more bold and italics text
traits.principle: Select the response that uses more bold and italics text

recommendation.reason: Strongest signal in the data (33 of 36 models), but near-duplicate of structured formatting (same pick 95%, profile correlation 0.93). Keep this one instead if you prefer the more concrete wording; structured formatting has the human validation.

traits.name: has more structured formatting
traits.principle: Select the response that has more structured formatting

recommendation.reason: Relevant in 55%, 31 models significant, good human agreement (κ 0.55).

closest_traits.name: uses more bold and italics text

traits.name: more actively engages with the user
traits.principle: Select the response that more actively engages with the user

recommendation.reason: Strong signal (29 models) but vague: it contains the follow-up question (94% of those cases, same pick 98%) and otherwise tracks friendlier tone (profile correlation 0.87) and personal pronouns (0.87).

closest_traits.name: uses more personal pronouns (I, we, you)

traits.name: is more verbose
traits.principle: Select the response that is more verbose

recommendation.reason: Exact opposite of “is more concise”. Close to a coin flip: concise is relevant slightly more often (78% vs 70%) and its votes depend less on response order (21% vs 29%). Human agreement is the same for both (κ 0.43). Keep verbose instead if you prefer the wording.

closest_traits.name: uses more bold and italics text

traits.name: provides a numbered list format
traits.principle: Select the response that provides a numbered list format

recommendation.reason: Sub-case of structured formatting (70% of its cases, same pick 87%). In 28.5% of comparisons both responses use numbered lists, so the annotator abstains almost as often as it picks. Strong signal on its own though (27 models).

closest_traits.name: uses more bold and italics text

traits.name: ends with a follow-up question
traits.principle: Select the response that ends with a follow-up question

recommendation.reason: Relevant in 28%, 24 models significant. Concrete and checkable, and the second least order-dependent trait (22%). Human κ is low (0.26) because one annotator rarely marked it.

traits.principle: Select the response that uses a more enthusiastic tone

traits.principle: Select the response that uses more emojis

traits.principle: Select the response that compliments the user's question or prompt

traits.name: uses more humour
traits.principle: Select the response that uses more humour

traits.principle: Select the response that actively engages the reader with rhetorical questions

traits.name: uses more mathematical symbols and notation
traits.principle: Select the response that uses more mathematical symbols and notation

recommendation.reason: Depends on the topic of the prompt more than on the model. Relevant in 15%, significant for 10 models. Feels out of place next to tone and style traits.

traits.name: acknowledges own limitations or uncertainty more
traits.principle: Select the response that acknowledges own limitations or uncertainty more

recommendation.reason: Relevant in 13%, significant for 8 models, max strength 0.17. No duplicate, and the only uncertainty trait left if confident statements goes.

traits.name: includes more ethical considerations
traits.principle: Select the response that includes more ethical considerations

recommendation.reason: Weaker with the v3 annotator: relevant in 5.4%, significant for 6 models, max strength 0.09. Just above the rarely-relevant line. Kept because nothing else covers it.

closest_traits.name: is more empathetic to the user

traits.name: is more creative and original
traits.principle: Select the response that is more creative and original

recommendation.reason: Relevant in 33%, 33 models significant, up to 0.69. Somewhat evaluative, but no duplicate.

traits.name: is more factually correct
traits.principle: Select the response that is more factually correct

recommendation.reason: A quality judgement, not a personality trait, and the annotator cannot verify facts. Very strong signal in v3 (29 models, up to 0.58), which mostly ranks newer models above GPT-4o. In half of the cases where it votes, the vote flips with response order. Humans agree with each other on it reasonably (κ 0.59), but the annotator matches them worst of the ten validated traits (κ 0.22): it finds the trait relevant on 31 of 101 comparisons against 19 for the humans, and picks the same response in 8 of the 10 shared cases.

traits.name: is more concise
traits.principle: Select the response that is more concise

recommendation.reason: The one to keep from the length pair: relevant in 78% of comparisons, 28 models significant, and the least order-dependent of the frequent traits (21%). Close call against verbose.

traits.name: is more polite
traits.principle: Select the response that is more polite

recommendation.reason: 87% of its cases are friendlier-tone cases with the same pick in 93%. The two human annotators barely agreed on it (κ 0.12), and the annotator's vote flips with response order in two thirds of the cases where it votes at all.

traits.name: makes more confident statements
traits.principle: Select the response that makes more confident statements

recommendation.reason: Fails both reliability checks: human κ 0.10, and the annotator's vote flips with response order in 57% of all comparisons (69% of those where it votes). The surviving votes still give a strong signal (27 models), so reword and re-validate it if you want confidence covered.

closest_traits.name: uses more bold and italics text

traits.name: uses more casual language
traits.principle: Select the response that uses more casual language

recommendation.reason: 26 models significant, all above GPT-4o, up to 0.53. The vote flips with response order in 61% of the cases where it votes, which costs relevance (11.5%) but the surviving votes are consistent. Opposite pick to formal language in 99% of shared cases, but they share only 19% of their cases.

traits.name: expresses more emotion
traits.principle: Select the response that expresses more emotion

recommendation.reason: Near-duplicate of enthusiastic tone (same pick 96%, profile correlation 0.93) at about the same relevance and signal. Keep either one; enthusiastic is the more specific wording.

traits.name: uses more personal pronouns (I, we, you)
traits.principle: Select the response that uses more personal pronouns (I, we, you)

recommendation.reason: A word-count proxy, not a trait a reader would name. Its model ranking follows friendlier tone (0.89) and “actively engages” (0.87). Strong signal though (21 models), so a close call.

traits.principle: Select the response that more strictly follows the requested output format

recommendation.reason: Relevant in 5.6% of comparisons. Low human agreement (κ 0.12) and the most order-dependent of the non-rare traits (73%). Only meaningful when the prompt requests a format.

traits.principle: Select the response that has a more avoidant tone

traits.principle: Select the response that agrees more with the user

traits.principle: Select the response that suggests illegal activities

traits.name: contains less harmful information
traits.principle: Select the response that contains less harmful information

recommendation.reason: Relevant in 0.3% of comparisons. The annotator's vote flips with response order in 28% of all comparisons, the clearest sign that it cannot apply this trait. Also the only trait phrased as “less of something”.

traits.name: refuses to answer the question
traits.principle: Select the response that refuses to answer the question

recommendation.reason: Relevant in 1.3% of comparisons and not significant for any model, so it fails your first criterion on this prompt set. Close call because it is a clear behaviour with the highest human agreement of all traits (κ 0.74); worth keeping if new prompts will elicit refusals.
